title: Network Types, Topologies and Devices: From PAN to Spine-Leaf, and Hub to Firewall
intro: Network types, topologies and devices describe how networks are classified by scale and ownership (PAN, LAN, CAN, MAN, WAN, WLAN, SAN, the internet), how they are laid out (bus, star, ring, mesh, tree, hybrid, spine-leaf), and which equipment moves and controls traffic (NIC, hub, bridge, switch, router, Layer 3 switch, access point, firewall, load balancer, proxy, IDS/IPS, modem). The goal of this lesson is to let you look at any alert and say which device saw the traffic, which collision and broadcast domains it crossed, and what that device can and cannot tell you.

sections.heading: Network types by scale: PAN, LAN, CAN, MAN and WAN
sections.content:
A network type answers one question: how big is this network, and who owns it? Scale and ownership matter to an analyst because they decide three practical things: how much latency to expect, who can hand you logs, and how much you can trust the traffic on the wire.

**The five classic scales**

| Type | Typical range | Who owns it | Typical latency | Where a SOC analyst meets it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PAN (Personal Area Network) | about 1 to 10 m (Bluetooth class 2), up to ~100 m (class 1) | One person | a few ms | A phone tethered to a laptop, Bluetooth peripherals, a smartwatch pairing |
| LAN (Local Area Network) | One floor or building, copper runs up to 100 m per segment | The organization | well under 1 ms | Switch port logs, VLANs, lateral movement between workstations |
| CAN (Campus Area Network) | Several buildings of one organization, roughly 1 to 5 km | The organization (it owns or leases the fiber between buildings) | about 1 ms | A university or hospital campus, building-to-building fiber, campus Wi-Fi |
| MAN (Metropolitan Area Network) | A city or metro region, roughly 5 to 50 km | A carrier or municipality, leased to customers | about 1 to 5 ms | Metro Ethernet or dark fiber linking offices in the same city |
| WAN (Wide Area Network) | Countries and continents | Carriers; organizations lease capacity | about 10 to 300 ms (satellite can reach 600 ms) | Site-to-site VPN tunnels, MPLS or SD-WAN circuits, the internet edge |

**How to read the table**

- The dividing line is ownership as much as distance. You own your LAN and your campus cabling, so you can put sensors anywhere. You do not own a carrier's MAN or WAN, so you see only what arrives at your edge device (a router or firewall) plus whatever the carrier chooses to report.
- Technology does not define the type. The same Ethernet frames run in a LAN, over a metro fiber, and across a WAN circuit. What changes is distance, the party operating the link, and the contractual guarantees (a service-level agreement, SLA).
- Latency is physics plus equipment. Light in fiber covers roughly 200 km per millisecond, so a round trip between Tel Aviv and the US East Coast cannot beat about 80 ms, and real paths usually measure 100 to 130 ms. A LAN has no such delay.
- Boundaries are fuzzy. A large hospital may call its campus a LAN in conversation. What matters is the question you are asking: who runs this segment and can I get its logs?

**Common misconceptions**

- 'WAN means the internet.' No. A WAN is any wide-area network. A private MPLS circuit between two company offices is a WAN and never touches the public internet.
- 'A PAN is harmless.' A paired Bluetooth device or a phone hotspot creates a path that bypasses the corporate firewall entirely. A laptop connected to both the corporate LAN and a personal hotspot becomes an unmonitored bridge between the two.

**What to ask as an analyst**

1. Which scale does this traffic cross: did it stay inside one LAN, cross the campus backbone, or leave through the WAN edge?
2. Who owns the segment where something looks wrong, and is that the team or provider that can give me logs?
3. Is the observed latency consistent with the path I think the traffic took? A reply in 2 ms from a host claimed to be on another continent should make you question the claim.

**Scenario:** An alert shows a workstation sending data through a phone hotspot. Recognizing that a PAN or tether is involved tells you the traffic never crossed the firewall, so the firewall logs will be empty and you must pivot to endpoint telemetry.

sections.heading: WLAN, SAN and the internet as a network of networks
sections.content:
Three more network types do not fit the pure size ladder: they are defined by the medium, the purpose, or the way many networks are joined together.

**WLAN (Wireless LAN)**

A WLAN is a LAN whose last hop is radio, standardized as IEEE 802.11 (marketing names Wi-Fi 5, Wi-Fi 6/6E, Wi-Fi 7).

- Indoor range is typically 30 to 50 m per access point, and walls, glass, and interference cut that sharply.
- The air is a shared, half-duplex medium: only one device per channel transmits at a time, so capacity is divided among everyone near that access point. Wi-Fi uses collision avoidance (CSMA/CA) rather than the collision detection of old wired Ethernet.
- Clients join a named network (SSID), carried by a radio identified by a BSSID (usually the access point's MAC address). One SSID can be broadcast by dozens of access points.
- Logically a WLAN is not a separate kind of network: each SSID is normally mapped onto a VLAN of the wired LAN, so a Wi-Fi laptop and a wired desktop can sit in the same broadcast domain.
- Anyone within radio range can hear the signal, so a WLAN adds threats that wired ports lack: rogue access points, evil-twin SSIDs, and forged deauthentication frames (management frames that kick a client off, mitigated by 802.11w protected management frames).

**SAN (Storage Area Network)**

A SAN is a dedicated, high-speed network whose only job is to connect servers to block storage (disks presented to a server as raw volumes). It is deliberately separate from the user LAN.

- Transports: Fibre Channel (commonly 16, 32 or 64 Gbps, with its own switches and zoning), iSCSI (SCSI over TCP, port 3260, on ordinary Ethernet), or NVMe over Fabrics.
- It needs very low and predictable latency (well under 1 ms) and lossless behavior, because a stalled disk can crash a database.
- Pitfall: a SAN is not a NAS. A NAS (Network Attached Storage) serves files over the normal LAN with SMB or NFS; a SAN serves raw blocks over a dedicated storage fabric.
- Analyst relevance: ransomware operators go after storage arrays, snapshots, and backup targets. Changes to SAN zoning, deletion of snapshots, or unexpected administrative logins to a storage array are high-value signals, and iSCSI flows appearing from a user subnet are almost always wrong.

**The internet**

The internet is not a single network. It is a network of networks: tens of thousands of independently operated autonomous systems (ISPs, cloud providers, enterprises, universities), each identified by an AS number, exchanging reachability information using the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP).

- No one owns it. Each operator runs its own network and agrees to carry traffic for others under peering or transit contracts.
- It is best effort: nothing guarantees delivery, latency, or path. Two packets in one conversation may even take different routes.
- It is untrusted by definition. Every external source address is controlled by someone you do not know.

**Terms that are often confused**

- Intranet: a private network using internet technology (web servers, email), reachable only by the organization.
- Extranet: an intranet slice deliberately shared with partners or customers, usually behind authentication.
- VPN: not a network type but a virtual overlay. It builds a logical private network across a public one by encrypting and encapsulating traffic.

**What to ask as an analyst**

- Which AS and country does this external address belong to, and does that fit the business relationship?
- Is this storage or backup traffic crossing a boundary it should never cross?
- Which SSID and access point did this device use, and is that SSID one we operate?

sections.heading: Topologies: bus, star, ring, mesh, tree and hybrid
sections.content:
A topology is the shape of a network. There are two views, and mixing them up is the most common mistake.

- Physical topology: how cables and devices are actually laid out (what you would see in a wiring closet).
- Logical topology: how data actually flows between nodes, regardless of the cabling.

A network can be physically one shape and logically another. Keep that distinction in mind for the next section.

**The classic shapes**

- **Bus.** All nodes tap a single shared backbone cable (10BASE5 and 10BASE2 coaxial Ethernet, with 50-ohm terminators at both ends). Cheap and simple, but every node hears every transmission, collisions are constant, and one cable break or missing terminator corrupts the whole segment. One faulty NIC that transmits endlessly can silence everyone.
- **Star.** Every node has its own cable to a central device (hub or switch). A cable failure takes down only that node, and troubleshooting is easy. The weakness is the center: if the central device dies, everything attached to it dies (a single point of failure).
- **Ring.** Each node connects to exactly two neighbors, forming a loop. Token Ring (IEEE 802.5) passed a token so only the holder could transmit. FDDI used two counter-rotating fiber rings so a break could be healed by wrapping traffic onto the second ring. Rings survive today in carrier and metro networks (SONET/SDH rings and Ethernet Ring Protection, ITU-T G.8032), which restore service within tens of milliseconds after a cut.
- **Mesh.** Nodes interconnect with many links. In a full mesh every node links to every other, so the number of links is n(n-1)/2: 5 nodes need 10 links, 10 nodes need 45, and 50 nodes need 1,225. It is the most resilient and the most expensive. In a partial mesh only important nodes get multiple links, the practical choice for WANs.
- **Tree (hierarchical).** A star of stars: access devices connect to distribution devices, which connect to a core. It scales well and keeps traffic organized, but a failure of an upstream node isolates everything beneath it unless links are doubled.
- **Hybrid.** A combination of the above. Every real enterprise network is hybrid: star in the closet, tree across the building, partial mesh across the WAN.

**Comparison**

| Topology | Wiring | Failure behavior | Where you see it today |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bus | One shared cable | A break or fault affects the whole segment | Legacy serial and industrial buses, historical Ethernet |
| Star | Each node to a central device | Node cable failure hits one node; central failure hits all | Every office LAN |
| Ring | Each node to two neighbors | One break tolerated only with dual rings or a ring protocol | Carrier metro rings, some industrial rings |
| Full mesh | Every node to every other | Highly resilient; many paths | Small core clusters, tunnels between a few key sites |
| Partial mesh | Selected extra links | Resilient where it matters | Enterprise WAN, internet backbone |
| Tree | Layers of stars | Upstream failure isolates a subtree | Campus LAN (access, distribution, core) |
| Hybrid | Any combination | Depends on the mix | Nearly all real networks |

**Why the analyst cares**

Topology tells you where traffic must pass. In a tree, north-south traffic funnels through the core, so a sensor there sees a lot. In a mesh there may be many paths, so a sensor on one link may miss half the conversation (asymmetric routing). In a star, the central device is also where you place visibility, and where an attacker aims to cause an outage.

**Questions to ask:** What is the single point of failure here? If this link fails, what path does traffic take, and will my sensor still see it?

sections.heading: Modern Ethernet and the spine-leaf data center
sections.content:
Early Ethernet really was a bus: 10BASE5 and 10BASE2 coax with every station on one wire. In 1990 the IEEE standardized 10BASE-T twisted pair, and wiring moved to a star centered on a hub. The hub repeated every signal to every port, so the network was physically a star but still logically a bus (one shared collision domain). Replacing hubs with switches finished the transformation.

**Why modern Ethernet is physically a star and logically switched**

- Physically a star: every device has its own cable (copper limited to 100 m, or fiber for longer runs) to a port on a switch in a wiring closet. This is structured cabling: wall jack, patch panel, switch, with a main distribution frame (MDF) and intermediate closets (IDF) per floor.
- Logically switched: the switch gives each port a dedicated, full-duplex path and forwards each frame only toward its destination. No sharing, no collisions, and one host cannot passively hear another host's unicast traffic.
- Why this won: a failed cable affects one device, bandwidth is not shared, ports can be monitored and controlled individually, and VLANs, port security, and 802.1X become possible per port.

**The loop problem and Spanning Tree**

Engineers add redundant uplinks so a single link failure is survivable. But redundant Layer 2 links form physical loops, and Ethernet frames have no hop counter. A broadcast sent into a loop circulates forever and multiplies: a broadcast storm that can saturate a network within seconds. The Spanning Tree Protocol (IEEE 802.1D, with faster Rapid STP in 802.1w) solves this by logically blocking redundant ports so the active topology is a loop-free tree, and unblocking a port when a link fails.

Analyst relevance: a sudden flood of broadcast traffic, switch CPU spikes, MAC addresses flapping between ports, and topology-change messages are the signature of a loop, whether accidental (someone plugs both ends of a patch cable into one switch) or deliberate.

**Spine-leaf: the data-center topology**

Traditional three-tier trees were designed for north-south traffic (users to servers). Modern data centers are dominated by east-west traffic (server to server: microservices, storage replication, virtual machine migration). Spine-leaf is built for that.

- Leaf switches are the access layer: servers, storage, and firewalls plug into leaves.
- Spine switches form the backbone. Every leaf connects to every spine. Leaves never connect to other leaves, and spines never connect to other spines.
- Any server to any server on a different leaf takes exactly two switch hops (leaf, spine, leaf) with a predictable delay.
- Traffic is spread across all spines in parallel using equal-cost multipath (ECMP). No link is blocked as STP would impose, because the fabric is routed at Layer 3 between leaf and spine.
- Scaling is simple: add spines for more bandwidth, add leaves for more ports.
- Oversubscription example: a leaf with 48 ports of 10 Gbps toward servers (480 Gbps) and 4 uplinks of 40 Gbps (160 Gbps) is oversubscribed 3:1.
- Isolation across the fabric is usually delivered by an overlay such as VXLAN with a BGP EVPN control plane, so what the server sees as one flat segment is actually encapsulated across a routed underlay.

**What this means for the analyst**

- East-west traffic inside a data center usually never touches a perimeter firewall. Unless microsegmentation or an internal firewall is deployed, lateral movement there can be nearly invisible to network logs.
- Overlay encapsulation means a capture on a spine shows the outer addresses of the leaf devices, not the real servers. You need to know where decapsulation happens.

**Questions to ask:** Where does east-west traffic get inspected? Which devices see the original addresses, and which see only the tunnel endpoints?

sections.heading: Layer 1 and Layer 2 devices: NIC, hub, bridge and switch
sections.content:
Network devices differ by how much of each packet they read before deciding what to do. The simplest read nothing; the smartest read the application payload. This section covers the devices that work at the physical and data-link levels (the layers themselves are taught in the OSI lesson; here we only use their names).

**NIC (Network Interface Card)**

The NIC is the endpoint's door into the network: a physical card, a motherboard chip, a USB dongle, a Wi-Fi radio, or a virtual NIC inside a virtual machine.

- It has a 48-bit MAC address, usually burned in by the manufacturer. The first 24 bits (OUI, Organizationally Unique Identifier) identify the vendor, which helps identify device types.
- By default it accepts only frames addressed to its own MAC, broadcasts, and joined multicasts. In promiscuous mode it accepts everything it hears, which is how sniffers work.
- The MAC is an identifier, not proof of identity: software can change it (MAC spoofing), and many devices randomize Wi-Fi MACs, so one phone may appear under several.

**Hub**

A hub is a multiport repeater (Layer 1). It receives a signal on one port and blindly repeats it out of every other port.

- All ports share one collision domain and half-duplex bandwidth (a 10 Mbps hub divides 10 Mbps among everyone).
- Every host sees every frame, so sniffing is trivial.
- Why it is obsolete: since the late 1990s switches cost about the same and deliver dedicated bandwidth per port, full duplex, and security features. You will still meet hubs in old industrial gear. Do not confuse a hub with a passive network TAP (a purpose-built device that copies traffic to a monitoring port) or with an inexpensive unmanaged switch.

**Bridge**

A bridge (Layer 2) connects two or a few segments, learns which MAC addresses live on which side, and forwards frames only when needed. It split big shared collision domains into smaller ones. The idea survives in software: Linux bridges, hypervisor virtual switches, container networking, and an access point bridging Wi-Fi to Ethernet.

**Switch**

A switch is a multiport bridge implemented in hardware (ASICs), the standard Layer 2 device.

- It keeps a MAC address table (also called the CAM table) of MAC, VLAN, and port. It learns by reading the source MAC of each incoming frame and forwards by looking up the destination MAC.
- Known unicast goes out one port. Unknown unicast and broadcast are flooded out all other ports in the VLAN.
- Entries age out (300 seconds by default on many Cisco switches), and tables hold a limited number of entries.
- In a MAC flooding attack, a tool such as macof sends thousands of frames with random source MACs, fills the table, and forces the switch to flood unicast traffic like a hub, letting the attacker sniff. Port security (limiting MACs per port) prevents it.
- Common features: VLANs (IEEE 802.1Q, IDs 1 to 4094), trunks, port security, 802.1X, DHCP snooping, dynamic ARP inspection, port mirroring (SPAN), Power over Ethernet (802.3af/at/bt), and Spanning Tree.
- An unmanaged switch has no logs and no configuration, so it is invisible to you. A rogue unmanaged switch under a desk is a classic way to extend a network around controls.

**Telemetry from these devices**

NICs surface in endpoint inventories (adapter name, MAC, link speed). Switches provide syslog (link up/down, port-security violations, MAC flapping, STP topology changes, 802.1X results), SNMP counters, and on better models flow records.

**Questions to ask:** Which switch and port is this MAC on? When did that MAC first appear, and did it move between ports?

sections.heading: Layer 3, wireless and edge devices: router, L3 switch, access point, WLC and modem
sections.content:
These devices connect separate networks together or connect different kinds of media. They are the seams of the network, and seams are where telemetry and attacks concentrate.

**Router**

A router works at Layer 3. It forwards packets between different networks by looking at the destination IP address and consulting its routing table (it picks the entry with the longest matching prefix).

- Each router interface belongs to a different network and is its own broadcast domain. By default the router does not forward Layer 2 broadcasts.
- Routes are directly connected, static, or dynamic (OSPF inside an organization, BGP between organizations).
- The router is each host's default gateway: the first hop for any destination outside its own network.
- Routers commonly apply access control lists (ACLs): stateless permit or deny rules on source, destination, protocol, and port, which can log their hits.
- Pitfall: a router forwards whatever the routing table and ACLs allow. A basic ACL has no concept of a session, so it is not equivalent to a stateful firewall.

**Layer 3 switch**

A Layer 3 switch is a switch that can also route in hardware, the heart of most campus networks.

- Inter-VLAN routing is done through switched virtual interfaces (SVIs), one per VLAN, at wire speed.
- Compared with a router it has many more ports at lower per-port cost, but fewer WAN interface types and weaker services such as VPN.
- Pitfall: a VLAN is a segmentation boundary only until something routes between VLANs. If the Layer 3 switch has no ACL, any VLAN can reach any other, and since the traffic never crosses the firewall, nothing is logged.

**Access point (AP) and wireless LAN controller (WLC)**

An AP bridges 802.11 radio to wired Ethernet and maps each SSID to a VLAN. Small sites use standalone APs. Enterprises use a WLC (or a cloud-managed platform) to manage many APs, commonly over CAPWAP tunnels (RFC 5415, UDP ports 5246 and 5247). The WLC centralizes client authentication (802.1X with a RADIUS server), roaming, RF management (channel and power), and rogue AP detection (wireless intrusion prevention, WIPS).

Telemetry: association and disassociation events, authentication results with reason codes, client MAC, SSID, BSSID, AP name, signal strength (RSSI), roaming, and rogue AP alerts.

**Modem**

A modem converts between the digital signals of your network and the signal of the access medium: DOCSIS over cable, DSL over phone lines, or an optical network terminal (ONT) for fiber. Home and small-office equipment often combines modem, router, switch, AP, and a basic firewall in one residential gateway, which is why people say modem when they mean the whole box. Remote workers sit behind consumer gateways you do not manage and cannot see into, so your visibility starts at the VPN or the endpoint agent.

**Summary**

| Device | Main layer | Boundary it creates | Typical telemetry |
|---|---|---|---|
| Router | 3 | Broadcast domain per interface | ACL hits, interface and routing events, config changes |
| L3 switch | 2 and 3 | Per-VLAN domains plus routing | ACL logs, port events |
| AP / WLC | 1 and 2 | Radio edge | Association, authentication, rogue AP alerts |
| Modem / gateway | 1 and 2 (more in combos) | Provider edge | Little, mostly link status |

**Questions to ask:** Which device routes between these two segments, and does it log? Is the client on a managed AP or an unknown one?

sections.heading: Security and traffic devices: firewall, load balancer, proxy and IDS/IPS
sections.content:
Some devices are not about getting packets from A to B but about deciding whether and how traffic should pass. They are the sources of the logs a SOC analyst reads most.

**Firewall**

A firewall enforces policy between network zones (for example inside, DMZ, outside).

- Stateful inspection: it tracks each connection (addresses, ports, protocol, state) in a session table. Return traffic for an allowed connection is permitted automatically, while unsolicited inbound packets are dropped.
- Policy is evaluated top to bottom, and the final rule is an implicit deny.
- Next-generation firewalls (NGFW) add application identification, user identity, URL filtering, TLS inspection, and intrusion prevention.
- Telemetry: allow and deny decisions, session start and end, bytes, rule name, zones, application, and user. Denies show attempts; allows show what actually got through and are usually the more important logs.
- Pitfall: a firewall only sees traffic that crosses it. Hosts in the same segment never reach it.

**Load balancer**

A load balancer presents one virtual address to clients and distributes connections across a pool of servers, using health checks to remove failed members. Layer 4 balancers decide using IP and port; Layer 7 balancers read HTTP, can route by URL or header, and often terminate TLS. Pitfall: the backend server sees the load balancer's address as the client, so the real client IP must be recovered from a header such as X-Forwarded-For.

**Proxy**

A proxy acts on behalf of someone else and opens its own connection to the destination.

- Forward proxy: sits in front of users, controls and logs outbound web access (user, URL, category, bytes, verdict), and may cache.
- Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers, hiding them, and often hosts a web application firewall (WAF) or content delivery features.
- The destination sees the proxy's address, not the client's, so proxy logs are where the real user-to-URL link lives.

**IDS and IPS sensors**

- IDS (Intrusion Detection System): passive. It analyzes a copy of traffic (from a SPAN port or a TAP) and raises alerts. It cannot stop anything.
- IPS (Intrusion Prevention System): inline. Traffic passes through it, so it can drop or reset a flow. If it fails, it either fails open (traffic continues, no protection) or fails closed (traffic stops).
- Detection is by signature (known patterns, such as Suricata or Snort rules) and by anomaly. Alerts carry a signature ID, message, addresses, and the action taken.
- Pitfall: an IDS alert about an exploit attempt does not prove compromise. Check whether the traffic was blocked upstream and whether the target responded.

**Switch vs router vs firewall**

| Property | Switch | Router | Firewall |
|---|---|---|---|
| Primary job | Connect devices inside one network | Connect different networks | Allow or deny traffic between zones |
| Decides using | Destination MAC address | Destination IP address | Policy: addresses, ports, state, application, user |
| Main layer | 2 (3 on L3 switches) | 3 | 3 to 7 |
| Bounds broadcasts | No (VLANs do) | Yes, per interface | Yes, at the zone boundary |
| Keeps state | MAC table only | Routing table | Session table |
| Key log | Port events, MAC moves | ACL hits, route changes | Allow and deny sessions |

In practice one box does several jobs: a branch router may include a firewall, and an NGFW routes. Learn the functions, not the product labels.

sections.heading: Collision domains and broadcast domains
sections.content:
Two terms describe how far a transmission reaches. Mixing them up leads to the wrong diagnosis.

**Collision domain**

A collision domain is a set of devices that share a medium such that two of them transmitting at the same time corrupt each other's signals. It matters only on half-duplex shared media: old bus networks, hub-based networks, and Wi-Fi (where a channel is shared by everything on it, handled with collision avoidance).

- A hub does not divide collision domains: all its ports form one.
- A bridge or switch gives every port its own collision domain.
- On full-duplex links (modern switch ports) collisions cannot happen at all, because each direction has its own wire pair. A collision counter above zero on a modern switch port is therefore a clue to a duplex mismatch (one side half duplex, the other full) or an old device.

**Broadcast domain**

A broadcast domain is the set of devices that receive a Layer 2 broadcast frame (destination MAC FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF) sent by any one of them.

- A switch does not stop broadcasts. It floods them within the VLAN.
- A VLAN splits one switch into multiple broadcast domains.
- A router interface bounds a broadcast domain, because routers do not forward Layer 2 broadcasts. Routing between VLANs lets two broadcast domains communicate without merging.

**Side-by-side comparison**

| Device or setup | Collision domains | Broadcast domains |
|---|---|---|
| Hub with N ports | 1 | 1 |
| Switch with N ports, one VLAN | N (one per port) | 1 |
| Switch with N ports split into V VLANs | N | V |
| Router with N interfaces | N (one per interface) | N |
| Wi-Fi AP on one channel | 1 (shared air) | 1 per SSID-to-VLAN mapping |

**Worked example**

A 24-port switch has 16 ports in VLAN 10 and 8 ports in VLAN 20, with a trunk to a router. Every port is its own collision domain, and because the links are full duplex, no collisions occur. The switch has 2 broadcast domains. A broadcast from a VLAN 10 host reaches the other VLAN 10 hosts and the router's VLAN 10 interface, and never reaches VLAN 20 hosts.

**Why broadcast domain size matters**

- Every host must process every broadcast, so a domain with hundreds of busy devices wastes CPU and bandwidth, and a loop turns it into a storm.
- Many attacks only work inside the same broadcast domain: ARP spoofing, rogue DHCP servers, LLMNR and NBNS poisoning, and several discovery scans. An attacker on another VLAN must first obtain a routed path through a policy point.
- Smaller domains give a smaller blast radius and force traffic across a Layer 3 device where it can be filtered and logged.

**Common mistakes**

- 'A switch separates networks.' It separates collision domains, not broadcast domains.
- 'VLANs are secure by themselves.' A VLAN is a logical broadcast boundary. Misconfigured trunks, native VLAN tricks, or double tagging (VLAN hopping) can leak across it, and an unfiltered Layer 3 switch routes between VLANs freely.

**Questions to ask:** Are the attacker and the victim in the same broadcast domain? If not, which routed device must the traffic have crossed, and what does its log show?

sections.heading: Where the analyst sees each device in the logs
sections.content:
Knowing the device is half the job. The other half is knowing what story its logs can tell and what they cannot. A device logs only what it forwards, decides, or observes.

**Typical high-level log content by device**

- **Switch.** Port-security violations (for example: Security violation occurred, caused by MAC address aaaa.bbbb.cccc on port Gi1/0/12, often followed by the port going err-disabled), link up/down, MAC addresses flapping between ports (a loop or spoofing sign), 802.1X results, DHCP snooping and dynamic ARP inspection drops, STP topology changes, and configuration changes.
- **Router.** ACL hit logs (for example: list 110 denied tcp 198.51.100.23(44123) -> 192.0.2.10(3389), 1 packet), interface up/down, routing adjacency changes, and administrator configuration changes.
- **Access point / WLC.** Client association and disassociation, authentication results with reason codes, SSID, BSSID, AP name, client MAC, RSSI, roaming events, rogue AP detections, and deauthentication floods.
- **Firewall.** One record per session or deny: timestamp, source and destination address and port, protocol, action (allow, deny, drop, reset), rule, zones, bytes, application, and user for NGFWs.
- **Load balancer and proxy.** Client and backend address, URL, response code, bytes, and pool member health. These hold the client identity that other devices lost.
- **IDS/IPS.** Alerts with signature ID, message, severity, addresses, and whether the action was alert or block.

**Reading the evidence correctly**

| What you see | What it means | What it does not prove |
|---|---|---|
| Firewall deny from an external address | Policy stopped an attempt | Anything about other paths in |
| Firewall allow with large outbound bytes | Data left through an approved rule | That the data was legitimate (check destination, user, app) |
| Router ACL deny on a sensitive port | The attempt reached the router and was filtered | That no other interface offered a path |
| Port-security violation | An unexpected MAC appeared on a port | That the device is malicious (could be a new docking station) |
| Wi-Fi association from an unfamiliar MAC | A new device joined the SSID | Who owns it (MACs can be randomized) |
| IDS alert on an exploit signature | A pattern was observed | That the exploit worked |

**Blind spots every analyst should remember**

- Traffic between two hosts in the same VLAN on the same switch never reaches a firewall or router. Only the switch, an endpoint agent, or a sensor on that segment can see it.
- Encrypted or tunneled traffic (VPN, VXLAN) hides its inner details from devices on the path.
- Hosts behind NAT, a proxy, or a load balancer appear under the intermediary's address in downstream logs. Find the intermediary's own log to recover the original client.
- Consumer gateways and unmanaged switches produce no logs at all.
- All sources must agree on time. If one device's clock is off by a few minutes, correlating a switch event with a firewall session will mislead you. Confirm time synchronization (NTP) before building a timeline.

**A reusable questioning framework**

1. Which device saw this event, and at what point in the path?
2. What does that device see and decide, and what is invisible to it?
3. Which neighboring device should have logged the same activity from another angle?
4. Does the topology (star, tree, spine-leaf) explain why this device did or did not see the traffic?
5. Which broadcast domain are the endpoints in, and which routed device sits between them?

**Scenario:** An alert shows a workstation scanning internal hosts, but the firewall shows nothing. The targets are in the same VLAN, so the scan never crossed the firewall. The next step is to check the switch, the endpoint agent, and any internal sensor on that VLAN, not to conclude the scan did not happen.

quiz.question: You are investigating a suspected scan from one workstation to many other workstations. The perimeter firewall logs show no related traffic at all. All the hosts are in the same VLAN on the same access switch. What is the most accurate conclusion?

options.label: The scan never happened, since the perimeter firewall would have logged every workstation-to-workstation connection
The firewall log pipeline is broken, and no internal conclusion can be drawn until that collection is restored
Switched intra-VLAN traffic never reached the firewall, so pivot to the access switch, endpoint agent, or internal sensor
A router between the hosts silently dropped the traffic, which is why the perimeter firewall never recorded it

quiz.explanation: Frames between hosts in the same VLAN are forwarded at Layer 2 by the switch and never reach a firewall or router, so an empty firewall log is expected and visibility must come from the switch, an endpoint agent, or a sensor on that segment. Concluding the scan did not happen confuses absence of evidence from one device with evidence of absence. Assuming the firewall logging is broken is unjustified, because the device simply never saw this traffic. Blaming a router is wrong because same-VLAN traffic is not routed at all.

quiz.question: A company wants every one of its 8 sites to have its own direct link to every other site (a full mesh). How many point-to-point links are required, and what is the main drawback?

options.label: 8 links, because each site only needs one connection
28 links, and the cost and complexity grow quickly as sites are added
56 links, and a single failed site breaks the whole network
16 links, and the main drawback is that collisions become frequent

quiz.explanation: A full mesh needs n(n-1)/2 links, which is 8 x 7 / 2 = 28, and the count grows roughly with the square of the number of sites, which is why real WANs use a partial mesh. Eight links would give only a ring or similar shape, not a full mesh. Fifty-six double counts every link (each pair counted in both directions), and a full mesh is actually very resilient to a single failure. Sixteen has no basis in the formula, and collisions are a shared-medium issue unrelated to the number of dedicated point-to-point links.

quiz.question: An analyst sees a switch suddenly forwarding large amounts of unicast traffic out of many ports, and a sniffer on one port is capturing conversations between other hosts. Logs show thousands of new source MAC addresses learned on one port within seconds. What is happening?

options.label: A MAC flooding attack has filled the MAC address table, so the switch is falling back to flooding traffic like a hub
Spanning Tree has correctly blocked a redundant link, which is normal
The router's routing table has overflowed and is sending packets to the wrong network
A hub was added to the network, so collision domains have been split

quiz.explanation: Thousands of random source MACs from one port filling the CAM table is the signature of MAC flooding (for example the macof tool); once the table is full the switch floods unknown unicast out all ports, letting an attacker sniff, and port security limiting MACs per port is the fix. Normal Spanning Tree blocking does not cause flooding or new MACs. A routing table is a Layer 3 structure and has nothing to do with MAC learning on a switch. Adding a hub would not create thousands of learned MACs, and a hub merges collision domains rather than splitting them.

quiz.question: A router has three interfaces. Each interface connects to a separate switch, and each switch carries a single VLAN with 40 hosts. How many broadcast domains exist, and why?

options.label: One, because all the switches are connected to the same router
Two, because routers only separate two networks at a time
Zero, because switches stop broadcasts
Three, because each router interface bounds its own broadcast domain

quiz.explanation: Routers do not forward Layer 2 broadcasts, so each interface (with its switch and VLAN) is a separate broadcast domain, giving three. Saying one treats the router like a hub or a switch, which would merge the segments and defeat the purpose of routing. A router is not limited to separating two networks, so two is wrong. Switches do not stop broadcasts at all, they flood them inside the VLAN, so zero is wrong.

quiz.question: An IDS sensor connected to a SPAN port raises a high-severity alert for an exploit attempt against an internet-facing web server. What should the analyst conclude and do first?

options.label: The exploit was blocked automatically, because an IDS sensor drops malicious packets inline before they can arrive
The server is already compromised, so isolate it at once and skip any further log verification for the moment
The alert is a false positive, since a sensor on a SPAN port sees only copied traffic and cannot inspect sessions
The attempt was observed but not necessarily blocked or successful, so verify with firewall, server and endpoint logs

quiz.explanation: An IDS watches a copy of the traffic and only alerts; it cannot block, and a signature match shows an attempt, not success, so you correlate with the firewall, the web server or load balancer logs, and endpoint telemetry to see whether it reached the target and what the reply was. Claiming it was blocked confuses an IDS with an inline IPS. Declaring compromise without evidence skips the verification step an alert always needs. Calling it a false positive is wrong because a SPAN-fed IDS sees real traffic copies; it is just not proof of impact.
